newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Crude contracts hold back Australia refinery cuts.
newsitem.headline: Crude contracts hold back Australia refinery cuts.

text.p: Australian refiners have not cut refining output despite losses due to prior crude purchase commitments, industry sources said on Thursday.

"No one is cutting back crude rates yet," a refining source said. "All the refiners have booked crude for February and March arrival. (There is) very little they can do to cut rates," one refining source said.

The source said most refiners are operating at nearly 100 percent capacity with one refiner, Australian Petroleum Pty Ltd (APPL) which trades as Ampol operating at close to 90 percent due to delays in crude arrival.
He said some refiners might operate at lower rates because "a few cargoes were delayed by the weather" but these are not definite yet.
Australian refiners were said to be sufffering fates similar to their Singapore counterparts as margins slump to negative levels.
"(Margins) at the moment are pretty dreadful. Margins are negative," the source said.
But refiners will only be able to lower runs sometime in the second half of March or April if the losses persist, he said.
Plumetting oil product prices in Singapore led to almost immediate announcements of reduction in crude run by two refiners early this week.
Shell Singapore cut runs at its 435,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery by 30,000 bpd last Friday. Esso Singapore reduced output over the weekend by 20 to 25 percent at its 230,000 bpd refinery.
Singapore Refining Co (SRC) was also planning a 15-day cut in production this week by between 10,000 and 15,000 bpd.
Sources said some refiners in South Korea are also thinking of lower operating rates as they grapple with the poor margins and dwindling demand for their high export volume.

Thai refiners who are already operating on average of about 10-percent below capacity are also contemplating further output cuts. Refiners there said cuts might be effected as early as February if there were no signs of weakening crude prices.
Crude prices have in fact strengthened with NYMEX WTI crude gaining 21 cents per barrel to last trade at $24.45 on the after-hours ACCESS system.

For the moment, Australian refiners are also able to operate at current high rates because they have to make up for production losess suffered by a few refiners in December due to plant problems, the source said.
"In the last couple of months some had cracker problems and are operating to meet requirements," he said.
Australian petroleum demand peaked just before the Christmas holidays and will remain relatively high for the next one to two months of the summer driving season.
